name: Carijona
confidence_why: Robayo 1989, the language's fieldworker, states penultimate word stress outright and no source gives a different placement, but his is the only rule on record: Meira 1998 declined to say anything about Karijona stress because the stress marks in Koch-Grünberg 1908 and Huber & Reed 1992 are inconsistent, and Koch-Grünberg 1908 notes that a word's stress often shifts in sentence context.

new_statements.quote: Meira 1998:19: "As for Karihona, Kh1 (the most reliable source for phonology) does not mark stress; Kh2 and Kh3 often have stress marks, but they are inconsistent and frequently in disagreement. Because of this, nothing can be said here about stress in Karihona." [Kh1 = Robayo 1986, 1987; Kh2 = Huber & Reed 1992; Kh3 = Koch-Grunberg 1908, per Table 1, p.4.] Meira 1998:57: "Due to the absence of Karihona data, Proto-Taranoan stress will remain unreconstructed." Koch-Grunberg 1908:955: "Die Betonung eines Wortes ist häufig verschieden, je nachdem es allein ausgesprochen oder in einem Satz gebraucht wird."
new_statements.translation: Koch-Grunberg 1908:955: 'The stress of a word is often different depending on whether it is pronounced alone or used in a sentence.'

new_statements.rule_in_words: No published rule for the position of word stress in Carijona was found. The only first-hand remark (Koch-Grunberg 1908, Hianakoto-Umaua dialect) says word stress shifts between citation form and sentence context without saying where it falls; the only modern comparative treatment (Meira 1998) explicitly declines to state anything because the sources' stress marks (Koch-Grunberg 1908, Huber & Reed 1992) disagree and Robayo does not mark stress. The sister languages Tiriyo and Akuriyo have iambic rhythmic stress (Meira 1998:18), but Meira does not extend this to Karihona.
new_statements.domain_note: Koch-Grunberg's remark contrasts isolation (citation) forms with sentence context, implying phrase-level effects on word accent; no word-level rule given.
new_statements.identity_note: Koch-Grunberg 1908 describes the Hianakoto-Umaua of the Macaya/Cunyary (upper Apaporis), which he and later authors (Durbin & Seijas 1973; Meira 1998:7) treat as a dialect of the same language as Carijona/Guaque; Glottolog files it under cari1279. Meira 1998 uses the spelling Karihona; Guerrero-Beltran uses Karijona (Puerto Nare, Guaviare). All refer to cari1279.

new_statements.quote: Les phonèmes / ï / et / e / se réalisent [ ϖ ] et [ √ ], ils acquièrent un trait de postériorité à la suite de consonnes vélaires. L'accent vient sur la pénultième syllabe du mot.
new_statements.translation: The phonemes /ï/ and /e/ are realised [ɨ] and [ʌ]; they acquire a back feature after velar consonants. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word.
new_statements.citation: Robayo, Camilo. 1989. "En faisant une rame": texte carijona. Amerindia 14. Paris: Association d'Ethnolinguistique Amerindienne.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 14 pages, text layer). extracted text of PDF p.3 gives, immediately after the vowel table: "Les phonèmes / ï / et / e / se réalisent [ ϖ ] et [ √ ], ils acquièrent un trait de postériorité à la suite de consonnes vélaires. L'accent vient sur la pénultième syllabe du mot." — identical to the reader's quote (the text layer's "[ √ ]" is a font artefact; the 300-dpi render shows "[ ʌ ]", so the reader's translation [ɨ]/[ʌ] is right). A a full-text search for stress/accent all 14 pages for accent/pénulti/syllabe/tonique/prosod hits only these two lines (116-117), so it is the sole stress statement in the work. The sentence is an unconditioned penultimate rule with no weight, secondary-stress or…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate: penultimate stress) and as the existing statement's reading 'fixed: penultimate syllable'. It is the only first-hand explicit stress rule for Carijona found so far; it supersedes Meira 1998's 'nothing can be said here about stress in Karihona', which did not use this source.3 mentions accent/pénultième/syllabe).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the penultimate syllable; a one-sentence statement with no conditions, no weight reference, no exceptions.
new_statements.exceptions: none mentioned; the Carijona forms in the text and glosses carry no stress marks (all acute/grave marks in the PDF text are French orthography), so the statement cannot be checked against the data in the same work
new_statements.identity_note: Robayo 1989 describes the Carijona spoken near Miraflores (Comisaria del Guaviare, Colombia), from a text recorded in Bogota in 1986 with the speaker Horacio Carijona 'Nigua' (d. 1987); no dialect split is stated. Huber & Reed 1992 (not opened) would cover the Carijona (cbd) column of a comparative wordlist.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction between statements of placement, because only one source states a placement: Robayo 1989 (fieldworker, first-hand) gives penultimate word stress without qualification. The tension is one of confidence: Meira 1998 (pp.18-19, 57, already held by the project) declined to say anything about Karihona stress because Robayo's 1986/1987 manuscripts do not mark stress and the stress marks in Huber & Reed 1992 and Koch-Grunberg 1908 are inconsistent and disagree, and Koch-Grunberg 1908 (p.955) noted that the stress of a word often differs between isolation and sentence context. The catalog's penultimate rule therefore rests on Robayo 1989's single sentence.
